title: Can a Placebo Survive the Truth?
paragraphs: For most of medical history, the placebo was regarded as a polite deception. A physician who prescribed a sugar pill to a demanding patient was thought to be offering comfort rather than treatment, and the comfort depended on the patient never learning the truth. Much later thinking inherited this assumption, which reduces to a tidy rule: if a placebo works only through belief, then honesty must destroy it.

The rule looks less secure than it once did. In a small randomized trial published in two thousand and ten, researchers led by Ted Kaptchuk gave patients with irritable bowel syndrome pills that were openly described as placebos containing no active ingredient. Those patients reported more improvement than a comparison group that received no treatment. Yet the details matter: participants were also told that placebo pills had been shown to produce improvement in earlier clinical studies.

This detail is easy to overlook, and it complicates the triumphant reading. The patients were not deceived about the pill, but they were hardly left without expectations; honesty about the contents arrived together with persuasion about the effect. Whether that combination counts as fully informed consent, or merely as a more respectable form of suggestion, is a question the trial itself cannot answer.

None of this makes the old deception acceptable. The American Medical Association, for instance, advises physicians to obtain a patient's general consent before using a placebo in clinical practice, and the reasoning is not hard to reconstruct: trust in medicine is a shared resource that one convenient lie can quietly erode. The interesting shift is elsewhere: the ethical problem may lie less in the sugar pill than in how the conversation around it is conducted.

The open-label studies, then, do not show that belief is irrelevant; they suggest that belief and honesty need not be enemies. That is a more modest conclusion than enthusiastic summaries sometimes imply, but it is also a more useful one. A placebo that survives the truth is still a placebo, yet it is one a doctor can prescribe without having to hope the patient never asks.

questions.prompt: What is the author's overall position?

options.text: Doctors should replace most drugs with placebos

options.text: Honesty and placebo effects may coexist
options.explanation: Yazar, inanç ile dürüstlüğün düşman olmak zorunda olmadığını ölçülü bir sonuç olarak sunar.

options.text: Placebos work only when patients are deceived
options.explanation: Metin tam da bu eski kuralın artık sağlam görünmediğini söyler.

options.text: Open-label trials have settled the ethical debate
options.explanation: Yazar onam sorusunu denemenin yanıtlayamayacağını vurgular; tartışma kapanmış değildir.

questions.prompt: Besides learning that the pills were inert, what were the open-label participants told?

options.text: That the pills had been proven to cure bowel syndrome in 2010

options.text: That the AMA had approved placebos for general clinical practice
options.explanation: AMA onay vermez, genel onam alınmasını önerir; ayrıca bu katılımcılara söylenmedi.

options.text: That the comparison group would be given a different placebo
That earlier studies had linked such pills to improvement
options.explanation: Katılımcılara plasebo haplarının önceki klinik çalışmalarda iyileşme sağladığı söylendi.
